I'm 36 years old and I've been farming these 50 mu in Quzhou since I was 21. My old man taught me the basics, and after 15 years I know what this land can handle. With seven people in my household—including my parents and two school-age kids—I need stable grain income first, but school fees and daily expenses force me to grow vegetables for cash. My well gives me reliable water, but pumping costs electricity, so I don't waste a single irrigation.

The wheat I sowed last October on 28 mu is greening up now. I'll top-dress urea at revival and irrigate four times: overwintering, jointing, heading, and grain filling. I plant improved Jimai varieties because they don't lodge in the spring winds and the grain buyer pays a fair price. Right after wheat harvest in early June, I'll no-till or lightly rotary-till and put in Zhengdan 958 hybrid maize—I've used it for ten years and it reliably gives me over 600 jin per mu with three irrigations.

Garlic on 8 mu is my big gamble for cash. It went in last autumn too, and it needs heavy potassium and five irrigations to fatten the bulbs before May harvest. I save my own cloves for seed—hybrid garlic seed is a rip-off—and after pulling garlic that land might get a rest unless I feel the soil is strong enough for a quick autumn crop.

I'm planting chili on 5 mu this year. My wife and parents can help pick, and the Shijiazhuang buyer comes to the village edge. Hybrid chili costs more for seedlings but resists virus and yields twice the local open-pollinated types. Onion on 4 mu is steady money—the broker from the county town always takes it. I'll put autumn cabbage on 3 mu after the garlic comes out or on my south plot; it stores in the cellar if prices are low at harvest.

My 2 mu of stevia I've kept going for three years now. A buyer from Tianjin pays decent money for dried leaves, and it doesn't fight me like vegetables do. I give it less fertilizer than the others and irrigate four times through the summer.

For all the plots, I rotary till—deep ploughing burns too much diesel and the soil here is heavy loam that packs down anyway. I spray pesticides when I see damage, not by the calendar, but vegetables need more protection than grain. Fertilizer prices have been high, so I don't overdo it: base dressing with compound fertilizer at sowing, then top-dress by growth stage. I've learned that cheaping out on nitrogen mid-season costs more in lost yield than the bag of urea costs.
